newsitem.title: FRANCE: Solana promises France major NATO role.
newsitem.headline: Solana promises France major NATO role.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Monday promised France a major role in the Atlantic Alliance command structure once it returns to full integration into NATO's military wing, which it left in 1966.

Solana endorsed calls by French President Jacques Chirac and the United States for a summit of NATO's 16 nations, east European candidates for membership and Russia in mid-1997 to approve a new security architecture for Europe.
He also made clear he expected some Western peacekeeping troops to stay in Bosnia after the NATO-led peace implementation force's mandate expires at the end of the year.
"France's role will be very, very important. It must play a role proportionate to its capabilities and its importance," Solana said after talks with Chirac which he described as very constructive.
"I hope we will be able to find a solution so that France as well as Spain, which are moving closer to NATO, can be comfortable in the new command structure," he said.

Diplomatic sources said France is in tough negotiations with both European allies and the United States on the role of the Western European Union defence grouping, and of French officers, in a reformed NATO military wing.

Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said the president had stressed the need for practical arrangements "to give the necessary political visibility and operational capability to a European defence identity".

French Defence Minister Charles Millon called this month for the appointment of a European deputy to the U.S. Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), who would command WEU military operations in which the United States chose not to participate.
The diplomats said Paris sought that role for itself and was also interested in one of NATO's regional commands in Europe.
Millon told reporters after meeting Solana: "The French are not reasoning in terms of the posts they will hold but in terms of the balance between Europe and the United States."
At present the three NATO area commands in Europe are held by British, German and U.S. officers.

The Naples-based post of commander-in-chief of allied forces in southern Europe, now held by a U.S. admiral, interests the French, but Washington wants to keep it tied to command of the U.S. Sixth Fleet in the Mediterranean, diplomats said.

The newspaper Liberation reported on Monday that Paris had dismissed the offer of a new southwest European command covering its own territory, the Iberian peninsula and the Atlantic approaches, saying nothing ever happened there.

General Charles de Gaulle pulled France out of the alliance's military wing in 1966 in protest at U.S. domination. Chirac took the first step towards full participation last year when he agreed to France's defence minister and chief of staff attending NATO meetings for the first time in three decades.
Diplomats said the key issue was the degree of autonomy which European forces would have in running their own military operations and the extent of remaining American control.
In a speech at the French Senate, Solana called for reformed NATO command structures to enable European allies to take greater responsibility.

But he also noted that due to budget constraints, European members would not have the resources to sustain complex military interventions in the near future and would anyway want to act in most cases along with the United States through NATO.
On enlargement, Solana said he hoped a decision naming the first new countries to be admitted to NATO would be taken at the summit in mid-1997.
The NATO chief and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov came no closer to compromise on Friday on NATO's plans, opposed by Moscow, to admit ex-Soviet bloc states as members.

However, Colonna said Chirac had noted there was now broad support for the idea of "a new organisation of peace on the European continent", which could take the form of a NATO pact with Russia to wipe out the effects of the 1945 Yalta division of Europe and avoid creating new fault lines.
